analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share vehicle data and repair tools with independent shops and owners.
analysis.headline: The House subcommittee advanced the bipartisan REPAIR Act by voice vote in February 2026, but the full committee and the House have not yet voted.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar carmakers from using technological or legal barriers to keep owners, independent repair shops, and aftermarket parts makers from getting vehicle data and critical repair information. Carmakers would have to share diagnostics and repair tools on the same terms they share them with dealers and authorized shops, and the Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules. It also creates an advisory committee on repair competition, requires a consumer-education rule from highway safety regulators, and overrides state laws covering the same ground.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners, independent repair shops, and aftermarket parts and tool makers. Owners get the legal right to their vehicle's repair data and to choose any shop, towing service, or parts brand. Independent shops and parts makers get access to the same diagnostics and software that dealers use, so they can compete on repairs instead of losing work to dealer service centers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: A manufacturer may not use any technological or legal barrier that prevents an owner or an independent shop from accessing vehicle-generated data and critical repair information, including software and calibration tools.

Carmakers must provide owners and independent shops the same data, through the vehicle's diagnostic port or wirelessly, in the same manner and at the same cost as they provide it to dealers and authorized service providers.
Manufacturers may not require waivers of the owner's right to choose a repair shop, and may not mandate the use of particular parts or tool brands except for recall and warranty repairs.

People who receive vehicle data may not use it for unrelated purposes or sell it, and must delete it within 72 hours of an owner's request, with an exception only for de-identified research and development.

The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the law and handle complaints from any person, with orders that can be appealed to federal court, and NHTSA would write rules telling buyers about these rights at the point of sale.

analysis.who_pays: Vehicle manufacturers and their dealer service networks. They would lose their exclusive grip on repair data, software, and diagnostics, and would bear the cost of sharing that information on equal terms. The bill also preempts state laws covering the same subject, which takes away states' ability to set their own repair rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local laws covering the same subject, so states could not maintain their own vehicle repair or data rules, including stronger ones already on the books.

Requiring manufacturers to share repair data through ports and wireless systems creates real cybersecurity and safety concerns that the bill acknowledges but only partially addresses, allowing makers to keep protections for safety-critical systems.

Manufacturers and dealers argue that opening vehicle data access increases risk of hacking or tampering with safety systems; the bill limits what must be shared and excludes fully self-driving vehicles.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: cheaper repair options and a working competitive market for parts and service, which independent shops and consumer groups have sought for years. The real costs fall on manufacturers, who must build data-sharing systems and give up a lucrative service monopoly. The main design weakness is preemption: if a state wanted stronger protections, this bill would override them, and critics in good faith point to cybersecurity risk from widened data access. On balance, the consumer and small-business benefits outweigh the compliance costs, though the state-law override is a genuine trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared its House subcommittee by voice vote in February 2026 and is now waiting for the full Energy and Commerce Committee and then the House floor; no further vote has happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Neal Dunn introduced the bill on February 25, 2025 with 15 original cosponsors from both parties, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and its Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade subcommittee.
The bill collected 45 cosponsors, 23 Democrats and 22 Republicans, making it one of the more broadly bipartisan repair bills in the House.
On February 10, 2026, the subcommittee held a mark-up session and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote.
No full committee vote or House floor vote has taken place, and the bill remains with the Energy and Commerce Committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and their dealer service networks, who keep exclusive control of repair data and software as long as the bill sits unpassed in committee. Consumer and independent-repair interests got a procedural win at the subcommittee stage but no change in practice yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, while the bill waits in committee

for.name: Rep. Neal Dunn
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the REPAIR Act on February 25, 2025 and gathered 15 original cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: 45 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, giving the bill a nearly even bipartisan base in the House.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade
for.role: Subcommittee with jurisdiction over the bill
for.what_they_did: Held a mark-up session on February 10, 2026 and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (full committee)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-KY)
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a markup or vote on the bill since the subcommittee forwarded it in February 2026.

against.name: Automakers and dealer networks
against.role: Vehicle manufacturers and dealership service industry
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed right-to-repair legislation, arguing expanded data access creates security and safety risks, and have lobbied against similar measures in Congress and states.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 45 cosponsors split almost evenly, 23 Democrats and 22 Republicans, and a Republican sponsor paired with a bipartisan subcommittee vote shows support crossing party lines.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that clear a subcommittee but sit waiting for full committee action rarely reach the floor unless the committee chair schedules a markup. With more than a year left in the Congress, the bill's strong bipartisan cosponsorship keeps it alive, but the odds still favor it stalling in committee rather than becoming law in this session.
